questions.q: Does a CSV column header need to exactly match a Salesforce API field name?
options: Yes, or the import rejects the entire file immediately
No — both tools let you map a file's column names to Salesforce fields during the import
Only for custom fields, never for standard fields
Only when using Data Loader, never the Import Wizard
questions.explain: Column headers are mapped to Salesforce fields during the import step, so they don't need to match exactly — but every row still needs the same column count as the header.

questions.q: Which date format is safest to avoid ambiguity across both Salesforce tools?
options: dd-MM-yy
yyyy-MM-dd
Month DD, YYYY written out in full
Any format, since Salesforce auto-detects every date style
questions.explain: yyyy-MM-dd (e.g. 2026-03-14) is unambiguous and read correctly by both the Import Wizard and Data Loader, unlike mixing MM/dd/yyyy and dd/MM/yyyy.

questions.q: A Lead row has "Acme Corp, Inc." as the company name but it isn't wrapped in quotes. What happens on import?
options: Salesforce automatically detects and quotes it
The comma splits the value into two columns, shifting the rest of that row
The row is skipped silently with no error
Nothing — commas inside values are always safe unquoted
questions.explain: An unquoted comma inside a value creates an extra column, which pushes every subsequent column in that row out of alignment — a common cause of silently swapped data.

questions.q: Why export the 18-character version of a Salesforce record ID for an update or upsert file, rather than the 15-character version?
options: The 15-character version doesn't work at all in CSV files
The 18-character version is case-insensitive, making it safer against a spreadsheet program altering case
The 18-character version is required by law in the EU
There's no difference; either works identically in every case
questions.explain: The 15-character ID is case-sensitive, so any case change (which spreadsheet software sometimes introduces) breaks matching. The 18-character ID is case-insensitive and safer to carry through a round trip.

questions.q: Why save a CSV as UTF-8 before loading it?
options: UTF-8 is required for files larger than 10 MB
It preserves accented or non-English characters that another encoding can corrupt
It automatically compresses the file for faster upload
It's only relevant for Data Loader, not the Import Wizard
questions.explain: A CSV saved in the wrong encoding can turn accented characters like the one in "José" into garbled text on import — UTF-8 protects against that.
